Skill Descriptor: Describe and contribute thoughts, feelings, and experiences and compare to those of their peers.
Achievement Indicators:
Personal Perspectives: Communicate personal likes, dislikes, and values, recognizing how these shape decisions and impact reactions.
Perspectives of Others: Compare and contrast personal values and viewpoints with those of others while demonstrating basic empathy.
Year-End: The student consistently and independently shares thoughts, feelings, and values, explains how they shape decisions and reactions, and compares them with peers' views with empathy, including on topics that matter to them.
Student Statement: I can share what I think and notice what others think
Conditions: Familiar, low-stakes topics; partners or small groups; structured talk with sentence starters.
Look Fors:
## Personal Perspectives
- Shares likes, dislikes, and experiences with a reason when prompted or given a turn-taking structure.
## Perspectives of Others
- Restates what a partner said.
- Identifies whether a peer's view is the same or different.
- Shows respectful listening: waits, looks at the speaker, doesn't dismiss.
Awareness - Description: Gives a reason for a preference and notices whether a peer agrees.
Awareness - Student Quote: I like graphic novels because the pictures help me visualize it. She doesn't like them, but I do.
Evidence Opportunities: A "would you rather" partner talk, then: "Tell me one way your partner is like you and one way they're different."

Skill Descriptor: Describe and contribute thoughts, feelings, and experiences and compare to those of their peers.
Achievement Indicators:
Personal Perspectives: Communicate personal likes, dislikes, and values, recognizing how these shape decisions and impact reactions.
Perspectives of Others: Compare and contrast personal values and viewpoints with those of others while demonstrating basic empathy.
Year-End: The student consistently and independently shares thoughts, feelings, and values, explains how they shape decisions and reactions, and compares them with peers' views with empathy, including on topics that matter to them.
Student Statement: I can share why I think what I think
Conditions: Topics with some personal stake; small groups; less teacher structure.
Look Fors:
## Personal Perspectives
- Moves from preferences toward values, with support naming them.
- Connects a feeling or reaction to an experience.
- Contributes voluntarily, at least some of the time.
## Perspectives of Others
- Asks a follow-up question to understand a peer's view ("Why do you think that?").
- Explains a difference simply.
- Responds to a different view without shutting it down.
Awareness - Description: Links a peer's view to their experience.
Awareness - Student Quote: He thinks that because he has a little brother, and I don't.
Evidence Opportunities: A small-group discussion about a character's choice in a shared text, then a reflection: "Did anyone see it differently? Why do you think they did?"

Skill Descriptor: Describe and contribute thoughts, feelings, and experiences and compare to those of their peers.
Achievement Indicators:
Personal Perspectives: Communicate personal likes, dislikes, and values, recognizing how these shape decisions and impact reactions.
Perspectives of Others: Compare and contrast personal values and viewpoints with those of others while demonstrating basic empathy.
Year-End: The student consistently and independently shares thoughts, feelings, and values, explains how they shape decisions and reactions, and compares them with peers' views with empathy, including on topics that matter to them.
Student Statement: I can see how my values shape my reactions, and that others' do too
Conditions: Topics where people disagree; group and whole-class talk; mostly independent.
Look Fors:
## Personal Perspectives
- Names a value behind an opinion and begins to explain how it shaped a decision or reaction.
- Describes a reaction and why, often after the fact rather than in the moment.
## Perspectives of Others
- Compares and contrasts their view with a peer's.
- Shows basic empathy by describing how something might feel from another position, even when disagreeing.
- Still tends to need a prompt on more controversial or high-interest topics.
Awareness - Description: Names a value behind a choice and what might shape a peer's different one.
Awareness - Student Quote: I picked fairness over winning, so that's why I'd tell the truth. Maya picked winning because her team was counting on her.
Evidence Opportunities: A values-based discussion (a dilemma or class decision), then: "Explain a view different from yours as fairly as you can. What might have shaped it?"
Left for June: Doing this consistently and independently, in the moment, on topics that matter to them, and connecting values to decisions without a prompt.

Skill Descriptor: Express and support ideas and opinions with evidence.
Achievement Indicators:
Identify Evidence: Justify personal position using personal experiences and anecdotal evidence.
Evidence Credibility: Provide relevant examples to strengthen personal ideas and opinions.
Year-End: The student states a clear position in discussion and backs it with relevant personal experiences and examples that actually strengthen the point.
Student Statement: I can give a reason for what I think
Conditions: Familiar, low-stakes topics; partner talk; sentence starters ("I think... because...").
Look Fors:
## Identify Evidence
- States an opinion and gives one reason, often general ("because it's fun").
- Shares a personal experience when prompted: "Has that happened to you?"
## Evidence Credibility
- Offers an example, though it may be loosely connected or slightly off topic
Awareness - Description: Can say what their reason is.
Awareness - Student Quote: I think we should have pets in class because my dog makes me happy.
Evidence Opportunities: A "this or that" partner talk where each student gives a position and one reason; the teacher notes whether a reason was given and whether it connects.

Skill Descriptor: Express and support ideas and opinions with evidence.
Achievement Indicators:
Identify Evidence: Justify personal position using personal experiences and anecdotal evidence.
Evidence Credibility: Provide relevant examples to strengthen personal ideas and opinions.
Year-End: The student states a clear position in discussion and backs it with relevant personal experiences and examples that actually strengthen the point.
Student Statement: I can back up my opinion with something that happened
Conditions: Topics with some personal stake; small groups; fewer starters.
Look Fors:
## Identify Evidence
- Supports a position with a specific personal experience or anecdote, told briefly and on point.
- Gives more than one reason when prompted ("Is there another reason?").
## Evidence Credibility
- Chooses examples that mostly connect to the opinion.
- Begins to notice when an example doesn't fit and drops it, with support.
Awareness - Description: Links the example to the opinion.
Awareness - Student Quote: Last year our class did a garden, and everyone helped, so that's why I think everyone would like a class project.
Evidence Opportunities: A small-group discussion on a class issue, with a quick exit slip: "What was your opinion? What example did you use?"

Skill Descriptor: Express and support ideas and opinions with evidence.
Achievement Indicators:
Identify Evidence: Justify personal position using personal experiences and anecdotal evidence.
Evidence Credibility: Provide relevant examples to strengthen personal ideas and opinions.
Year-End: The student states a clear position in discussion and backs it with relevant personal experiences and examples that actually strengthen the point.
Student Statement: I can choose an example that makes my opinion stronger
Conditions: Topics where peers disagree; group and whole-class talk; mostly independent.
Look Fors:
## Identify Evidence
- Justifies a position with relevant personal experience and anecdotal evidence, usually without prompting.
- Responds to a challenge by offering another example.
## Evidence Credibility
- Selects the more convincing of two examples when asked to choose.
- Examples are relevant, though sometimes still general rather than specific.
Awareness - Description: Begins to explain why an example helps.
Awareness - Student Quote: I used the late bus as my evidence because it happens a lot, which is a pattern.
Evidence Opportunities: A four-corners or mini-debate activity. Afterward: "Which example helped your side most? Why?"
Left for June: Consistently choosing relevant, specific examples on unfamiliar or contested topics, without a prompt to strengthen them.

Skill Descriptor: Summarize and present content to communicate facts, ideas, and opinions.
Achievement Indicators:
Content: Select information that supports purpose in a simple, organized structure.
Delivery: Present content in a manner that ensures the audience can follow along.
Year-End: The student selects the information that fits the purpose, organizes it simply, and presents it so an audience can follow without confusion.
Student Statement: I can share the main things I learned
Conditions: Short shares (1 to 2 minutes) on a familiar topic; to a partner or small group; organizer provided.
Look Fors:
## Content
- Retells information, often including more than is needed.
- Follows a given organizer (beginning, middle, end, or topic and three facts).
## Delivery
- Speaks loudly enough for a small group and looks up from notes some of the time.
- May read notes word for word.
Awareness - Student Quote: I told them three facts about wolves.
Evidence Opportunities: A partner "teach-back" after a short reading; the listener retells one fact they heard.

Skill Descriptor: Summarize and present content to communicate facts, ideas, and opinions.
Achievement Indicators:
Content: Select information that supports purpose in a simple, organized structure.
Delivery: Present content in a manner that ensures the audience can follow along.
Year-End: The student selects the information that fits the purpose, organizes it simply, and presents it so an audience can follow without confusion.
Student Statement: I can pick what's important and put it in order
Conditions: 2 to 3 minute presentations; small group or class; a simple visual allowed.
Look Fors:
## Content
- Selects key facts or ideas, leaving out some unneeded detail.
- Uses a clear, simple structure (opening, points, closing) with some independence.
- Distinguishes facts from their own opinion when presenting both.
## Delivery
- Uses signal words (first, next, the most important) so listeners can follow.
- Speaks from notes or cue cards rather than reading a script.
Awareness - Description: Explains a selection choice when asked.
Awareness - Student Quote: I left out the part about their teeth because my talk was about how they hunt.
Evidence Opportunities: A short research share with a peer checklist: "Could you tell the main idea? Could you follow the order?"

Skill Descriptor: Summarize and present content to communicate facts, ideas, and opinions.
Achievement Indicators:
Content: Select information that supports purpose in a simple, organized structure.
Delivery: Present content in a manner that ensures the audience can follow along.
Year-End: The student selects the information that fits the purpose, organizes it simply, and presents it so an audience can follow without confusion.
Student Statement: I can present so my audience can follow me
Conditions: Presentations to the class on a chosen or assigned topic; multimodal options; mostly independent planning
Look Fors:
## Content
- Selects information that supports a stated purpose; occasional extra detail remains.
- Organizes content into a structure that fits the purpose (steps, reasons, compare).
## Delivery
- Checks in with the audience (pauses, a question, a visual) to keep them following.
- Recovers from a stumble and continues, with some reliance on notes.
Awareness - Description: Connects delivery choices to the audience.
Awareness - Student Quote: I showed the picture first, so they'd know what a pangolin looks like before I explained.
Evidence Opportunities: A class presentation with audience exit slips ("What were the main points?"). Compare the slips to the presenter's plan.
Left for June: Selecting tightly for purpose without extra detail, and adjusting delivery in the moment when the audience seems lost.

Skill Descriptor: Use language of harmony and respect, self-monitoring and adjusting as appropriate.
Achievement Indicators:
Respectful Communication: Use language that demonstrates consideration for the feelings of others.
Self-Monitoring & Adjustment: Recognize when emotions and tone impact communication and show willingness to adjust.
Year-End: The student uses considerate language in most interactions, notices when their emotions or tone are affecting a conversation, and is willing to adjust.
Student Statement: I can use kind words when I talk with others
Conditions: Calm, structured partner and group work; class norms posted and practised.
Look Fors:
## Respectful Communication
- Uses polite basics (please, thank you, taking turns) in structured talk.
- Disagrees using provided sentence stems  ("I see it differently because...").
## Self-Monitoring & Adjustment
- Recognizes, when the teacher points it out, that tone affected how something landed.
- Can name a feeling they had during a conversation, after the fact.
Awareness - Student Quote: I was frustrated when they didn't listen to my idea.
Evidence Opportunities: Observations during group work against class norms; a brief reflection: "How did your group talk to each other today?"

Skill Descriptor: Use language of harmony and respect, self-monitoring and adjusting as appropriate.
Achievement Indicators:
Respectful Communication: Use language that demonstrates consideration for the feelings of others.
Self-Monitoring & Adjustment: Recognize when emotions and tone impact communication and show willingness to adjust.
Year-End: The student uses considerate language in most interactions, notices when their emotions or tone are affecting a conversation, and is willing to adjust.
Student Statement: I can notice how I'm saying something
Conditions: Group tasks with some real disagreement; less teacher structure.
Look Fors:
## Respectful Communication
- Disagrees respectfully without a frame most of the time.
- Acknowledges others' ideas before adding their own ("That's a good point, and...").
## Self-Monitoring & Adjustment
- Recognizes, with a prompt, when their tone or volume changed and how others reacted.
- Rephrases when asked ("Can you say that another way?").
Awareness - Student Quote: When I said it loud, she stopped talking. I think it sounded mean.
Evidence Opportunities: A group-work self-assessment with a scenario check: "Here's something a student said. How might it make someone feel? How could it be said differently?"

Skill Descriptor: Use language of harmony and respect, self-monitoring and adjusting as appropriate.
Achievement Indicators:
Respectful Communication: Use language that demonstrates consideration for the feelings of others.
Self-Monitoring & Adjustment: Recognize when emotions and tone impact communication and show willingness to adjust.
Year-End: The student uses considerate language in most interactions, notices when their emotions or tone are affecting a conversation, and is willing to adjust.
Student Statement: I can catch myself and fix how I said it
Conditions: Discussions on topics students care about; group and whole-class; mostly self-managed.
Look Fors:
## Respectful Communication
- Uses considerate language even when disagreeing on topics they care about, most of the time.
- Chooses words to be mindful of upsetting or leaving someone out.
## Self-Monitoring & Adjustment
- Notices on their own, sometimes during the conversation, when emotion is affecting their tone.
- Takes a step to adjust: pauses, rephrases, or apologizes.
Awareness - Student Quote: I was getting mad, so I stopped and said it again calmer.
Evidence Opportunities: Observation during a high-interest discussion, followed by a short reflection: "Was there a moment you changed how you were talking? What made you notice?"
Left for June: Self-monitoring consistently in the moment, including in heated situations, without a prompt.

Skill Descriptor: Ask and respond to questions to clarify information, explore possibilities, and identify solutions to a problem.
Achievement Indicators:
Clarify: Ask appropriate follow-up questions to clarify their understanding of the speaker's purpose.
Extend: Draw on prior knowledge, when possible, to aid in extending their understanding of the message.
Year-End: The student asks follow-up questions that clarify a speaker's purpose and uses what they already know to extend the conversation toward possibilities and solutions.
Student Statement: I can ask when I don't understand
Conditions: Partner or small-group talk on familiar content; question stems provided.
Look Fors:
## Clarify
- Asks basic clarifying questions about details ("What did you mean by...?" "Can you say that again?").
- Answers a question from a peer directly, with some extra detail.
## Extend
- Shares a related experience when asked "Does that remind you of anything?"
Awareness - Student Quote: I didn't get which day it was, so I asked.
Evidence Opportunities: A partner interview with stems; the teacher notes how many follow-up questions are asked and of what kind.

Skill Descriptor: Ask and respond to questions to clarify information, explore possibilities, and identify solutions to a problem.
Achievement Indicators:
Clarify: Ask appropriate follow-up questions to clarify their understanding of the speaker's purpose.
Extend: Draw on prior knowledge, when possible, to aid in extending their understanding of the message.
Year-End: The student asks follow-up questions that clarify a speaker's purpose and uses what they already know to extend the conversation toward possibilities and solutions.
Student Statement: I can ask questions to understand what someone means
Conditions: Small groups; topics with a problem to discuss; fewer stems.
Look Fors:
## Clarify
- Asks follow-up questions to seek the speaker's reason or purpose ("Why do you think that matters?").
- Paraphrases to check understanding ("So you're saying...?").
## Extend
- Connects what they hear to something they know, with occasional prompting.
- Asks "what if" questions to explore an idea.
Awareness - Student Quote: I asked why because I wanted to know if she was trying to convince us.
Evidence Opportunities: A problem-solving group task with an observer recording question types (clarify, extend, solve).

Skill Descriptor: Ask and respond to questions to clarify information, explore possibilities, and identify solutions to a problem.
Achievement Indicators:
Clarify: Ask appropriate follow-up questions to clarify their understanding of the speaker's purpose.
Extend: Draw on prior knowledge, when possible, to aid in extending their understanding of the message.
Year-End: The student asks follow-up questions that clarify a speaker's purpose and uses what they already know to extend the conversation toward possibilities and solutions.
Student Statement: I can use questions and what I know to work toward a solution
Conditions: Real class problems or text-based dilemmas; groups; mostly independent.
Look Fors:
## Clarify
- Asks appropriate follow-up questions to clarify a speaker's purpose without stems, most of the time.
- Responds to questions with answers that address the question asked.
## Extend
- Draws on prior knowledge to suggest possibilities ("We tried something like that in science...").
- Uses questions to move a group toward a solution, though this is yet to be even across groups and topics.
Awareness - Description: Links prior knowledge to the message.
Awareness - Student Quote: I knew about recycling from last year, so I asked if the school already has bins.
Evidence Opportunities: A class problem-solving discussion; afterward: "Which question helped your group most? What did you already know that helped?"
Left for June: Clarifying a speaker's purpose and drawing on prior knowledge consistently, across topics and groups, without prompting.

Skill Descriptor: Give and respond to a variety of directions and instructions.
Achievement Indicators:
Give: Give clear, step-by-step instructions in familiar contexts.
Follow: Follow multi-step, complex instructions, asking for clarification when necessary.
Year-End: The student gives clear, ordered instructions for familiar tasks and follows multi-step, complex instructions, asking for clarification when needed.
Student Statement: I can follow and give simple steps
Conditions: 2 to 3 step tasks; familiar routines; instructions given orally and in writing.
Look Fors:
## Give
- Explains a familiar routine (packing a bag, a game rule) in a mostly correct order.
- May skip steps that seem obvious to them.
## Follow
- Follows 2- to 3-step instructions, often checking with the teacher or a peer for confirmation.
- Asks for help when stuck, though often general rather than a specific step.
Awareness - Description: Notices a missed step after the fact.
Awareness - Student Quote: I forgot to tell him to turn it over first.
Evidence Opportunities: A "draw what I describe" partner task: one student describes a simple shape design, the other draws it. Compare results.

Skill Descriptor: Give and respond to a variety of directions and instructions.
Achievement Indicators:
Give: Give clear, step-by-step instructions in familiar contexts.
Follow: Follow multi-step, complex instructions, asking for clarification when necessary.
Year-End: The student gives clear, ordered instructions for familiar tasks and follows multi-step, complex instructions, asking for clarification when needed.
Student Statement: I can give steps someone else can follow
Conditions: 3 to 5 step tasks; some oral-only instructions; less familiar contexts.
Look Fors:
## Give
- Gives steps in order, using sequence words (first, then, after that).
- Includes most necessary details, such as quantities or locations.
## Follow
- Follows 3 to 5 step oral instructions with occasional checking.
- Asks a specific clarifying question ("Do we glue it before or after we cut?").
Awareness - Student Quote: He got confused, so I added where to put the paper.
Evidence Opportunities: Students write and give instructions for a familiar process; a peer follows them exactly and notes where they got stuck.

Skill Descriptor: Give and respond to a variety of directions and instructions.
Achievement Indicators:
Give: Give clear, step-by-step instructions in familiar contexts.
Follow: Follow multi-step, complex instructions, asking for clarification when necessary.
Year-End: The student gives clear, ordered instructions for familiar tasks and follows multi-step, complex instructions, asking for clarification when needed.
Student Statement: I can handle longer instructions and give clear ones
Conditions: Multi-step tasks with conditions ("if... then"); oral instructions; new contexts for following, familiar ones for giving.
Look Fors:
## Give
- Gives clear, step-by-step instructions for a familiar process with few gaps.
- Checks the listener is following and adds a missing detail when needed.
## Follow
- Follows multi-step instructions with conditions, though may lose track of later steps.
- Asks for clarification in the moment rather than waiting until finished.
Awareness - Student Quote: I said 'the blue folder' because she doesn't know where we keep stuff.
Evidence Opportunities: A procedural task (a science set-up, a recipe, a game) given orally; observation of steps completed and questions asked. Students then teach the process to a peer.
Left for June: Following complex instructions accurately through to the end and giving clear instructions without needing listener feedback to fill gaps.

Skill Descriptor: Understand communication conventions for a diverse set of audiences.
Achievement Indicators:
Verbal: Use appropriate tone and volume, and begin varying vocabulary to suit different audiences.
Non-verbal: Display basic body language and appropriate eye contact while beginning to understand the importance of facial expressions in conveying emotion.
Year-End: The student uses a suitable tone and volume, uses some audience-specific vocabulary, shows basic body language and eye contact, and is beginning to understand how facial expressions convey emotion.
Student Statement: I can be heard and look at who I'm talking to
Conditions: Partner and small-group talk with peers; short class shares.
Look Fors:
## Verbal
- Uses a volume that fits the setting (partner vs. small group) with reminders.
- Uses the same everyday vocabulary with most audiences.
## Non-verbal
- Faces the speaker or listener and makes some eye contact.
- Recognizes obvious facial expressions (happy, angry, confused) in others.
Awareness - Student Quote: You should face the person so they know you're listening.
Evidence Opportunities: Observation during partner talk using a simple look-for list (volume, facing, eye contact).
Teacher Note: Consider scaffolds and adjustments for students with social, cognitive, or cultural needs.

Skill Descriptor: Understand communication conventions for a diverse set of audiences.
Achievement Indicators:
Verbal: Use appropriate tone and volume, and begin varying vocabulary to suit different audiences.
Non-verbal: Display basic body language and appropriate eye contact while beginning to understand the importance of facial expressions in conveying emotion.
Year-End: The student uses a suitable tone and volume, uses some audience-specific vocabulary, shows basic body language and eye contact, and is beginning to understand how facial expressions convey emotion.
Student Statement: I can change how I talk for who I'm talking to
Conditions: Peers and familiar adults; mix of informal and more formal settings (a class share, talking to the principal).
Look Fors:
## Verbal
- Adjusts tone and volume between settings with less reminding.
- Begins to change word choice for an adult or younger audience ("Can I ask you something?" vs. "Hey").
## Non-verbal
- Uses open body language and appropriate eye contact in short presentations.
- Notices how a facial expression changes the meaning of what someone says, with prompting.
Awareness - Student Quote: I'd say it differently to my grandma than to my friends.
Evidence Opportunities: A role-play of the same message to two audiences (a friend and a teacher); students and observers note what changed.
Teacher Note: Consider scaffolds and adjustments for students with social, cognitive, or cultural needs.

Skill Descriptor: Understand communication conventions for a diverse set of audiences.
Achievement Indicators:
Verbal: Use appropriate tone and volume, and begin varying vocabulary to suit different audiences.
Non-verbal: Display basic body language and appropriate eye contact while beginning to understand the importance of facial expressions in conveying emotion.
Year-End: The student uses a suitable tone and volume, uses some audience-specific vocabulary, shows basic body language and eye contact, and is beginning to understand how facial expressions convey emotion.
Student Statement: I know the body talks too
Conditions: Varied audiences, including unfamiliar ones (a visitor, a younger class); presentations and conversations.
Look Fors:
## Verbal
- Uses appropriate tone and volume for most audiences without prompting.
- Varies vocabulary for an audience in planned situations; less consistently in spontaneous talk.
## Non-verbal
- Displays appropriate body language and eye contact in most settings.
- Explains how their own or others' facial expressions conveyed an emotion.
Awareness - Student Quote: I smiled when I said it so they'd know I was joking.
Evidence Opportunities: Students present to a younger class or a guest; self-reflection and observer notes: "What did you change for this audience? What did your face and body show?"
Left for June: Varying vocabulary in spontaneous talk, and using conventions consistently with unfamiliar audiences.
Teacher Note: Consider scaffolds and adjustments for students with social, cognitive, or cultural needs.

Skill Descriptor: Respond personally and critically to a variety of texts.
Achievement Indicators:
Personal Response: Express personal reactions and connections to oral and multimodal texts.
Analyze: Give a brief overview of the key details of oral and multimodal texts.
Year-End: After listening to or viewing a variety of texts, the student shares a personal reaction with a connection and gives a brief, accurate overview of the key details.
Student Statement: I can say what I thought of it
Conditions: Short videos, read-alouds, or podcasts (under 5 minutes); familiar genres; guided talk.
Look Fors:
## Personal Response
- Shares an overall reaction (liked, disliked, felt sad) with a simple reason.
- Makes a basic connection when prompted ("Has anything like this happened to you?").
## Analyze
- Retells what happened, often in order and with unnecessary detail.
Awareness - Student Quote: I liked the video because the things that happened were funny.
Evidence Opportunities: A turn-and-talk after a short video: "What did you think? What happened?"

Skill Descriptor: Respond personally and critically to a variety of texts.
Achievement Indicators:
Personal Response: Express personal reactions and connections to oral and multimodal texts.
Analyze: Give a brief overview of the key details of oral and multimodal texts.
Year-End: After listening to or viewing a variety of texts, the student shares a personal reaction with a connection and gives a brief, accurate overview of the key details.
Student Statement: I can pick out what matters and connect to it
Conditions: Longer and more varied texts (news clip, speech, infographic, short documentary); small-group discussion.
Look Fors:
## Personal Response
- Explains a reaction with a specific moment from the text.
- Makes connections to self, other texts, or the world with less prompting.
## Analyze
- Gives an overview that names the topic and two or three key details, leaving out most minor ones.
Awareness - Student Quote: It made me mad when they showed the garbage in the ocean because my family goes to the beach a lot.
Evidence Opportunities: A viewing guide with two columns (key details / my reaction), followed by a group share.

Skill Descriptor: Respond personally and critically to a variety of texts.
Achievement Indicators:
Personal Response: Express personal reactions and connections to oral and multimodal texts.
Analyze: Give a brief overview of the key details of oral and multimodal texts.
Year-End: After listening to or viewing a variety of texts, the student shares a personal reaction with a connection and gives a brief, accurate overview of the key details.
Student Statement: I can give a short overview and explain my response
Conditions: A variety of oral and multimodal texts, including some unfamiliar forms; independent response, then discussion.
Look Fors:
## Personal Response
- Expresses a reaction and connection that is clearly tied to the text, most of the time without prompts.
- Begins to question the text ("I wonder why they only showed one side").
## Analyze
- Gives a brief, mostly accurate overview of key details for familiar text types; may miss a key detail in unfamiliar forms.
Awareness - Description: Notices how the text affected them.
Awareness - Student Quote: The music got sad right before they told us the numbers, so I felt worse.
Evidence Opportunities: A short oral or written response to a multimodal text: a three-sentence overview, plus "How did this text make you feel, and what in it made you feel that way?"
Left for June: Accurate overviews across unfamiliar forms, and consistently connecting reactions to specific features of the text.

Skill Descriptor: Adjust interactions to reflect the situation, audience, and purpose.
Achievement Indicators:
Situational: Recognize that different situations require changes in communication and adjustments in tone, depending on the purpose.
Engagement: Identify different audiences and the appropriate language of each.
Year-End: The student recognizes how situation and purpose call for changes in tone and communication, and identifies different audiences and the language suited to each.
Student Statement: I know school talk and friend talk are different
Conditions: Clear-cut contrasts (playground vs. classroom, friend vs. principal); teacher-provided examples.
Look Fors:
## Situational
- Recognizes that some situations need different talk (quiet library voice, formal assembly).
- Identifies tone in an example as "friendly," "bossy," or "polite," with support.
## Engagement
- Names two or three audiences they talk to differently (friends, teachers, family).
Awareness - Student Quote: You don't talk to the principal like you talk to your friends.
Evidence Opportunities: Sentence sort of example sentences into "to a friend" and "to a teacher," with one reason for each placement.
Teacher Note: Int 6.7 focuses on using conventions; this descriptor focuses on recognizing when and why to adjust. The two pair well in the same tasks.

Skill Descriptor: Adjust interactions to reflect the situation, audience, and purpose.
Achievement Indicators:
Situational: Recognize that different situations require changes in communication and adjustments in tone, depending on the purpose.
Engagement: Identify different audiences and the appropriate language of each.
Year-End: The student recognizes how situation and purpose call for changes in tone and communication, and identifies different audiences and the language suited to each.
Student Statement: I can tell what type of communication a situation needs
Conditions: Less obvious contrasts (comforting vs. convincing a friend; a class debate vs. a group chat); role-play.
Look Fors:
## Situational
- Recognizes that purpose (to persuade, to apologize, to explain) changes tone, not just audience.
- Identifies a mismatch in a scenario ("That's too casual for a thank-you to a guest speaker").
## Engagement
- Identifies features of language for different audiences (word choice, slang, formality, length).
Awareness - Student Quote: If you're saying sorry, you have to sound serious or they won't believe you.
Evidence Opportunities: Role-play cards (same message, different situation or purpose); the audience identifies what changed and whether it fit.
Teacher Note: Int 6.7 focuses on using conventions; this descriptor focuses on recognizing when and why to adjust. The two pair well in the same tasks.

Skill Descriptor: Adjust interactions to reflect the situation, audience, and purpose.
Achievement Indicators:
Situational: Recognize that different situations require changes in communication and adjustments in tone, depending on the purpose.
Engagement: Identify different audiences and the appropriate language of each.
Year-End: The student recognizes how situation and purpose call for changes in tone and communication, and identifies different audiences and the language suited to each.
Student Statement: I can plan how to talk for a situation and audience
Conditions: Real or simulated situations with a purpose (inviting a guest, explaining to younger students, a class meeting); planning, then doing.
Look Fors:
## Situational
- Plans adjustments to tone for a known situation and purpose before speaking.
- Recognizes in reflection when their tone didn't fit and what they would change.
## Engagement
- Identifies audience and chooses appropriate language in planned interactions; spontaneous adjustments are less consistent.
Awareness - Student Quote: The kindergartners won't know 'recycle,' so I'll say 'put it in the blue bin.'
Evidence Opportunities: Students plan and deliver a short message to a real audience (another class, a staff member), then reflect: "Who was your audience? What did you change and why?"
Left for June: Recognizing and adjusting across a wider range of situations, including unplanned ones.
Teacher Note: Int 6.7 focuses on using conventions; this descriptor focuses on recognizing when and why to adjust. The two pair well in the same tasks.

Skill Descriptor: Critically reflect on the contributions of others.
Achievement Indicators:
Message: Begin to express personal reflections on others' ideas, connecting them to one's own thoughts.
Impact: Demonstrate how new information affects the overall understanding of a topic.
Year-End: The student reflects on peers' ideas by connecting them to their own thinking and shows how new information from others has changed or deepened their understanding.
Student Statement: I can respond to what someone else said
Conditions: Structured discussions on familiar topics; response stems ("I agree with... because").
Look Fors:
## Message
- Responds to a peer's idea with agreement or disagreement and a simple reason.
- Repeats or restates a peer's idea before responding, with a stem.
## Impact
- Names one new thing they learned from a peer, when asked.
Awareness - Student Quote: I agree with Liam that we need more time, because I never finish.
Evidence Opportunities: An exit ticket after a discussion: "One idea from someone else. Do you agree? Why?"

Skill Descriptor: Critically reflect on the contributions of others.
Achievement Indicators:
Message: Begin to express personal reflections on others' ideas, connecting them to one's own thoughts.
Impact: Demonstrate how new information affects the overall understanding of a topic.
Year-End: The student reflects on peers' ideas by connecting them to their own thinking and shows how new information from others has changed or deepened their understanding.
Student Statement: I can connect other people's ideas to my thinking
Conditions: Small-group discussions about texts or topics with more than one view; fewer stems.
Look Fors:
## Message
- Connects a peer's idea to their own ("That's like what I was thinking, but...").
- Builds on an idea rather than only agreeing or disagreeing.
## Impact
- Identifies how a peer's information added to what they knew ("I didn't know that before").
Awareness - Student Quote: Ava said the character was scared, not mean. That made sense with what I thought about the ending.
Evidence Opportunities: A before-and-after thinking chart: students write their idea before a discussion, then add what they heard and how it connects.

Skill Descriptor: Critically reflect on the contributions of others.
Achievement Indicators:
Message: Begin to express personal reflections on others' ideas, connecting them to one's own thoughts.
Impact: Demonstrate how new information affects the overall understanding of a topic.
Year-End: The student reflects on peers' ideas by connecting them to their own thinking and shows how new information from others has changed or deepened their understanding.
Student Statement: I can show how what I heard changed what I think
Conditions: Discussions on complex or contested topics; group and whole-class; mostly independent.
Look Fors:
## Message
- Expresses personal reflections on others' ideas, connecting them to their own, with some prompting toward the why.
## Impact
- Explains how a specific piece of new information changed or confirmed their understanding of the topic, usually in reflection after discussion.
Awareness - Student Quote: At first I thought uniforms were bad, but when Jai talked about saving money, I'm not sure now.
Evidence Opportunities: A "my thinking shifted" reflection after a discussion: "What did you think before? What did you hear? What do you think now?"
Left for June: Reflecting on others' ideas and their impact during the discussion itself, and consistently explaining why their understanding changed.

Skill Descriptor: Begin to explain how advanced word structure can be used as a word-solving strategy.
Achievement Indicators:
Word Solving / Knowledge: Apply knowledge of syllable patterns to chunk and decode longer words.
Morphology & Etymology: Recognize and decode Anglo-Saxon morphemes (prefixes and suffixes) and how they affect word meaning.
Year-End: The student independently uses syllable patterns and Anglo-Saxon affixes to decode and make meaning of unfamiliar words in varied texts, and explains how and why the strategy worked.
Student Statement: I can take words apart.
Conditions: Familiar two-syllable words, mostly in isolation, with teacher cues.
Look Fors:
## Word solving/syllables
- Counts syllables by identifying vowel sounds.
- Divides two-syllable words (nap-kin, rab-bit, sub-ject) and reads each chunk.
- Divides compound words (fire-place, under-ground).
## Morphology / Anglo-Saxon affixes
- Finds the base word by peeling off inflectional suffixes (-s, -es, -ed, -ing, -er, -est).
- Recognizes the prefixes un-, mis-, over-, under- and gives their meaning in familiar words (unkind, misread).
- Explains simple meaning shifts: -less means "without," -ful means "full of."
Awareness - Student Quote: I covered up the -ing and read 'laugh.'
Evidence Opportunities: A sort of 15 to 20 words. The student marks syllable breaks, circles affixes, and reads the words aloud. For three words, they answer, "What does the prefix tell you?"

Skill Descriptor: Begin to explain how advanced word structure can be used as a word-solving strategy.
Achievement Indicators:
Word Solving / Knowledge: Apply knowledge of syllable patterns to chunk and decode longer words.
Morphology & Etymology: Recognize and decode Anglo-Saxon morphemes (prefixes and suffixes) and how they affect word meaning.
Year-End: The student independently uses syllable patterns and Anglo-Saxon affixes to decode and make meaning of unfamiliar words in varied texts, and explains how and why the strategy worked.
Student Statement: I can choose how to break a word
Conditions: Three- and four-syllable words, some in sentences; prompts rather than cues.
Look Fors:
## Word solving/syllables
- Divides three-syllable and longer words (cor-ner, sea-son, mar-ble).
- Flexes: if one split doesn't make a real word, tries another.
## Morphology / Anglo-Saxon affixes
- Reads and defines more suffixes (-ness, -ly, -y, -ish, -en, -ward, -hood, -ship) and prefixes (out-, fore-, be-).
- Handles words with more than one affix (un-help-ful-ness).
- Notices spelling changes at the joints: doubling (hopping), dropping silent e (hoping), y to i (happiness).
- Explains that some suffixes change a word's job (kind describes; kindness is a thing).
Awareness - Description: Names the strategy and the word part.
Awareness - Student Quote: I saw 'over' at the front and '-ed' at the end, so I read the middle first.
Evidence Opportunities: An unfamiliar-word read-aloud with think-aloud prompts, plus word building: "How many real words can you build from help? What does each affix change?"

Skill Descriptor: Begin to explain how advanced word structure can be used as a word-solving strategy.
Achievement Indicators:
Word Solving / Knowledge: Apply knowledge of syllable patterns to chunk and decode longer words.
Morphology & Etymology: Recognize and decode Anglo-Saxon morphemes (prefixes and suffixes) and how they affect word meaning.
Year-End: The student independently uses syllable patterns and Anglo-Saxon affixes to decode and make meaning of unfamiliar words in varied texts, and explains how and why the strategy worked.
Student Statement: I can use word structure to figure out words, and tell how I did it
Conditions: Unfamiliar words in shared class texts; occasional prompts.
Look Fors:
## Word solving/syllables
- Decodes most unfamiliar multisyllabic words in text, sometimes needing a cue ("Is there a part you know?").
- Combines strategies (affixes, then syllables, then context), though not always in an efficient order.
- Self-corrects when a word doesn't fit, more reliably with familiar patterns.
## Morphology / Anglo-Saxon affixes
- Uses known affix meanings to make a reasonable guess at a new word's meaning in context.
- Explains how an affix changed meaning for familiar affixes; less sure with layered or less common ones.
Awareness - Description: Accurately retells the process, usually when prompted; the why is emerging.
Awareness - Student Quote: I took off 'mis-' and '-ed' and read 'judge,' so it means judged wrong.
Evidence Opportunities: The student reads a passage with three or four seeded unfamiliar words, then conferences: "Pick one tricky word. Show how you figured it out."
Left for June: Explaining without a prompt, explaining why a strategy worked, and applying it flexibly across varied texts.

Skill Descriptor: Read an increasing variety of texts with accuracy and expression, both silently and aloud.
Achievement Indicators:
Expression: Read a variety of familiar texts with changes in intonation, tone, and volume.
Rhythm & Phrasing: Identify how the internal and end punctuation contribute to rhythm and phrasing.
Smoothness: Read familiar texts with hesitations that do not interfere with meaning, rehearsing and self-correcting when prompted.
Automaticity: Decode the high-frequency and two- and three-syllable words in a passage at a consistent pace.
Year-End: The student reads a variety of familiar texts accurately and expressively, uses punctuation to guide phrasing, self-corrects when prompted, and decodes common and multisyllabic words at a steady pace.
Student Statement: I can read a practised text smoothly
Conditions: Rehearsed, familiar texts; mostly narrative.
Look Fors:
## Expression
- Changes voice for dialogue or obvious emotion in a rehearsed text.
## Rhythm & Phrasing
- Stops at end punctuation; may read through commas.
## Smoothness
- Some word-by-word reading and long pauses on unfamiliar words; self-corrects some errors when prompted.
## Automaticity
- Reads high-frequency words automatically; slows noticeably on three-syllable words.
Awareness - Student Quote: There's a question mark, so my voice goes up.
Evidence Opportunities: A one-minute oral reading of a rehearsed passage, with a simple fluency rubric (expression, phrasing, smoothness, pace).

Skill Descriptor: Read an increasing variety of texts with accuracy and expression, both silently and aloud.
Achievement Indicators:
Expression: Read a variety of familiar texts with changes in intonation, tone, and volume.
Rhythm & Phrasing: Identify how the internal and end punctuation contribute to rhythm and phrasing.
Smoothness: Read familiar texts with hesitations that do not interfere with meaning, rehearsing and self-correcting when prompted.
Automaticity: Decode the high-frequency and two- and three-syllable words in a passage at a consistent pace.
Year-End: The student reads a variety of familiar texts accurately and expressively, uses punctuation to guide phrasing, self-corrects when prompted, and decodes common and multisyllabic words at a steady pace.
Student Statement: I can use punctuation to help me sound right
Conditions: Familiar texts in more genres (poetry, readers' theatre, informational); some less-rehearsed reads.
Look Fors:
## Expression
- Varies intonation and volume to show meaning, not just dialogue.
## Rhythm & Phrasing
- Pauses at commas and reads in meaningful phrases most of the time; can explain what a comma or dash does to the sound.
## Smoothness
- Hesitations are shorter and rarely change meaning; rereads to fix an error when prompted.
## Automaticity
- Decodes most three-syllable words at pace; longer words still cause occasional slowdowns.
Awareness - Student Quote: I paused at the comma so it didn't all run together.
Evidence Opportunities: Readers' theatre performance plus a short conference: "Show me a spot where punctuation changed how you read it."

Skill Descriptor: Read an increasing variety of texts with accuracy and expression, both silently and aloud.
Achievement Indicators:
Expression: Read a variety of familiar texts with changes in intonation, tone, and volume.
Rhythm & Phrasing: Identify how the internal and end punctuation contribute to rhythm and phrasing.
Smoothness: Read familiar texts with hesitations that do not interfere with meaning, rehearsing and self-correcting when prompted.
Automaticity: Decode the high-frequency and two- and three-syllable words in a passage at a consistent pace.
Year-End: The student reads a variety of familiar texts accurately and expressively, uses punctuation to guide phrasing, self-corrects when prompted, and decodes common and multisyllabic words at a steady pace.
Student Statement: I can read with expression that matches the meaning
Conditions: Familiar texts across varied genres, including some first reads of shared class texts; silent and oral.
Look Fors:
## Expression
- Matches tone and volume to meaning across most familiar texts.
## Rhythm & Phrasing
- Identifies how internal punctuation (commas, dashes, ellipses) shapes rhythm and applies it in rehearsed reading.
## Smoothness
- Hesitations seldom interfere with meaning; self-corrects when prompted and sometimes independently.
## Automaticity
- Reads three-syllable and familiar longer words at a consistent pace in familiar text; less consistent in a cold read.
Awareness - Student Quote: I read it slower and quieter because that's where the character is scared.
Evidence Opportunities: A recorded oral reading of a familiar passage the student chooses, with a self-assessment against the fluency rubric. Compare with November's recording.
Left for June: Consistent pace and phrasing across a wider variety of texts, including less-rehearsed ones.

Skill Descriptor: Recognize how different strategies are used to determine the meaning of words.
Achievement Indicators:
Strategy Flexibility: Practice using an array of strategies for new vocabulary, such as morphology, context, dictionary, and text features.
Semantic Knowledge: Begin to use contextual clues and generalized morphology to understand new words.
Figurative Language: Identify the literal and figurative meanings of words and phrases.
Year-End: The student practises several strategies for unknown words, uses context and word parts to build meaning, recognizes which strategy they used, and tells literal from figurative meaning.
Student Statement: I can try a strategy when I don't know a word
Conditions: Teacher-selected words in short texts; strategies modelled and practiced one at a time.
Look Fors:
## Strategy Flexibility
- Uses one or two go-to strategies (skip it, ask someone, look it up) when told to.
- Uses a glossary or bolded-word text feature when pointed to it.
## Semantic Knowledge
- Uses an obvious context clue (a definition right in the sentence) with support.
- Recognizes a familiar base word inside a longer word.
## Figurative Language
- Identifies common similes and idioms as "not meaning exactly what it says," with examples.
Awareness - Student Quote: I looked in the glossary.
Evidence Opportunities: A short passage with three underlined words; students write what each means and which strategy they used.
Teacher Note: Reading 6.11 focuses on decoding with word structure; this descriptor focuses on meaning. Morphology shows up in both.

Skill Descriptor: Recognize how different strategies are used to determine the meaning of words.
Achievement Indicators:
Strategy Flexibility: Practice using an array of strategies for new vocabulary, such as morphology, context, dictionary, and text features.
Semantic Knowledge: Begin to use contextual clues and generalized morphology to understand new words.
Figurative Language: Identify the literal and figurative meanings of words and phrases.
Year-End: The student practises several strategies for unknown words, uses context and word parts to build meaning, recognizes which strategy they used, and tells literal from figurative meaning.
Student Statement: I can use clues in the sentence and the word
Conditions: Shared class texts, including informational; a strategy anchor chart available.
Look Fors:
## Strategy Flexibility
- Practices three or four strategies (context, word parts, dictionary, text features) and uses more than one when the first doesn't work.
## Semantic Knowledge
- Uses context clues such as examples, contrast, or restatement to make a reasonable guess.
- Uses common prefixes, suffixes, and roots to build meaning.
## Figurative Language
- Explains the figurative meaning of common similes, metaphors, and idioms in context.
Awareness - Student Quote: It said 'unlike his timid sister,' so timid must mean the opposite of brave.
Evidence Opportunities: A word-detective log during independent reading: word, my guess, clue I used, check.
Teacher Note: Reading 6.11 focuses on decoding with word structure; this descriptor focuses on meaning. Morphology shows up in both.

Skill Descriptor: Recognize how different strategies are used to determine the meaning of words.
Achievement Indicators:
Strategy Flexibility: Practice using an array of strategies for new vocabulary, such as morphology, context, dictionary, and text features.
Semantic Knowledge: Begin to use contextual clues and generalized morphology to understand new words.
Figurative Language: Identify the literal and figurative meanings of words and phrases.
Year-End: The student practises several strategies for unknown words, uses context and word parts to build meaning, recognizes which strategy they used, and tells literal from figurative meaning.
Student Statement: I can pick the strategy that fits and explain it
Conditions: Varied class texts; unfamiliar words met in real reading; anchor chart faded.
Look Fors:
## Strategy Flexibility
- Chooses a strategy that fits the word and situation (e.g., checks for a glossary in a science text) with some independence.
- Confirms a guess with a second strategy, when prompted.
## Semantic Knowledge
- Combines context and word parts to arrive at a meaning, though may be thrown by subtle or misleading clues or shades of meaning.
## Figurative Language
- Distinguishes literal and figurative meaning in less familiar expressions and explains the figurative meaning.
Awareness - Student Quote: Context didn't help, so I broke it into parts: 'inter' means between.
Evidence Opportunities: A conference during independent reading: "Show me a word you figured out. Which strategy did you use? Why that one?"
Left for June: Choosing and confirming strategies independently across text types, and recognizing when a strategy has led them astray.
Teacher Note: Reading 6.11 focuses on decoding with word structure; this descriptor focuses on meaning. Morphology shows up in both.

Skill Descriptor: Construct meaning from a variety of texts considering the source, intended audience, and purpose.
Achievement Indicators:
Literal Understanding: Summarize text to demonstrate comprehension and respond to literal questions.
Inferential Understanding: Use comprehension and prior knowledge to make predictions and draw conclusions.
Text Intention: Determine the writer's purpose and draw conclusions to determine if it was achieved.
Year-End: The student summarizes a variety of texts, answers literal questions, makes supported predictions and conclusions, and judges whether the writer achieved their purpose for the intended audience.
Student Statement: I can tell what the text said
Conditions: Short, accessible texts; familiar genres; guided questions.
Look Fors:
## Literal Understanding
- Retells the main events or facts, often with too much detail.
- Answers literal questions by finding the answer in the text.
## Inferential Understanding
- Makes a prediction based on the title, pictures, or what just happened.
## Text Intention
- Names a general purpose (to entertain, inform, or persuade) when given the choices.
Awareness - Description: Points to the source of an answer.
Awareness - Student Quote: It says right here on page 3.
Evidence Opportunities: A short reading with literal questions and a "retell in five sentences" task.

Skill Descriptor: Construct meaning from a variety of texts considering the source, intended audience, and purpose.
Achievement Indicators:
Literal Understanding: Summarize text to demonstrate comprehension and respond to literal questions.
Inferential Understanding: Use comprehension and prior knowledge to make predictions and draw conclusions.
Text Intention: Determine the writer's purpose and draw conclusions to determine if it was achieved.
Year-End: The student summarizes a variety of texts, answers literal questions, makes supported predictions and conclusions, and judges whether the writer achieved their purpose for the intended audience.
Student Statement: I can sum it up and read between the lines
Conditions: Shared class texts in more genres (articles, short stories, ads); small-group and independent work.
Look Fors:
## Literal Understanding
- Summarizes main idea and key details in a few sentences, leaving out most minor details.
## Inferential Understanding
- Makes predictions and draws conclusions using text clues plus what they already know.
- Explains which clue led to the inference, when asked.
## Text Intention
- Identifies the purpose and the intended audience of a familiar text type, with a reason.
Awareness - Student Quote: It doesn't say she's nervous, but she keeps checking her phone, and I do that when I'm nervous.
Evidence Opportunities: A summary plus an "it says / I know / so I think" organizer.

Skill Descriptor: Construct meaning from a variety of texts considering the source, intended audience, and purpose.
Achievement Indicators:
Literal Understanding: Summarize text to demonstrate comprehension and respond to literal questions.
Inferential Understanding: Use comprehension and prior knowledge to make predictions and draw conclusions.
Text Intention: Determine the writer's purpose and draw conclusions to determine if it was achieved.
Year-End: The student summarizes a variety of texts, answers literal questions, makes supported predictions and conclusions, and judges whether the writer achieved their purpose for the intended audience.
Student Statement: I can figure out what the writer was trying to do
Conditions: More complex texts, including unfamiliar sources and forms; mostly independent.
Look Fors:
## Literal Understanding
- Summarizes accurately and concisely across most text types.
## Inferential Understanding
- Draws conclusions supported by text evidence and prior knowledge, though may overreach on less familiar topics.
## Text Intention
- Determines the writer's purpose and audience, considering the source.
- Begins to judge whether the purpose was achieved, with prompting ("Did it convince you? Why?").
Awareness - Student Quote: It's from the company that makes the drink, so of course they want you to buy it.
Evidence Opportunities: Two short texts on one topic from different sources; students summarize each, identify purpose and audience, and decide which one did its job better.
Left for June: Independently judging whether a writer achieved their purpose, and supported conclusions across unfamiliar texts.

Skill Descriptor: Adjust and use a variety of strategies to make meaning.
Achievement Indicators:
Attention Strategies: Use graphic organizers to identify the main ideas and supporting details.
Knowledge Strategies: Use context clues and prior knowledge to make predictions and assumptions.
Monitoring Strategies: Check regularly for understanding and notice when comprehension breaks down.
Year-End: The student uses organizers to sort main ideas from details, draws on context and prior knowledge to predict, monitors understanding regularly, and adjusts strategies when meaning breaks down.
Student Statement: I can use a tool to keep track of what I read
Conditions: Teacher-assigned organizer; short, accessible texts; strategies modelled.
Look Fors:
## Attention Strategies
- Completes a given organizer, though may list details as main ideas.
## Knowledge Strategies
- Makes predictions using obvious clues (title, headings, pictures).
## Monitoring Strategies
- Notices confusion at the end of a reading rather than during it.
- Uses one fix-up strategy (reread) when prompted.
Awareness - Student Quote: I read it, but I don’t really get it.
Evidence Opportunities: A main idea and details organizer for a short informational or narrative text, plus a self-rating: "How well did you understand? What was confusing?"

Skill Descriptor: Adjust and use a variety of strategies to make meaning.
Achievement Indicators:
Attention Strategies: Use graphic organizers to identify the main ideas and supporting details.
Knowledge Strategies: Use context clues and prior knowledge to make predictions and assumptions.
Monitoring Strategies: Check regularly for understanding and notice when comprehension breaks down.
Year-End: The student uses organizers to sort main ideas from details, draws on context and prior knowledge to predict, monitors understanding regularly, and adjusts strategies when meaning breaks down.
Student Statement: I can tell when I'm lost and do something about it
Conditions: Shared class texts; a choice of two or three organizers; stop-and-check points marked in the text.
Look Fors:
## Attention Strategies
- Separates main ideas from supporting details on an organizer, mostly accurately.
## Knowledge Strategies
- Combines context clues and prior knowledge to predict and make reasonable assumptions.
- Revises a prediction when new information appears.
## Monitoring Strategies
- Checks understanding at marked stopping points and names where it broke down.
- Uses two or three fix-up strategies (reread, read on, ask a question, visualize).
Awareness - Student Quote: I got lost when it started talking about the second scientist, so I went back.
Evidence Opportunities: Sticky-note monitoring during reading (✓ got it, ? confused, ! fixed it), reviewed in a conference.

Skill Descriptor: Adjust and use a variety of strategies to make meaning.
Achievement Indicators:
Attention Strategies: Use graphic organizers to identify the main ideas and supporting details.
Knowledge Strategies: Use context clues and prior knowledge to make predictions and assumptions.
Monitoring Strategies: Check regularly for understanding and notice when comprehension breaks down.
Year-End: The student uses organizers to sort main ideas from details, draws on context and prior knowledge to predict, monitors understanding regularly, and adjusts strategies when meaning breaks down.
Student Statement: I can choose and change strategies as I read
Conditions: Varied and more complex texts; student-chosen organizers; stopping points fade.
Look Fors:
## Attention Strategies
- Chooses an organizer that suits the text, with some guidance.
## Knowledge Strategies
- Makes predictions and assumptions that draw on both text and prior knowledge, and checks them as they read.
## Monitoring Strategies
- Notices breakdowns during reading, more consistently in familiar text types.
- Switches strategies when the first doesn’t work.
Awareness - Student Quote: Rereading didn’t help, so I made a quick timeline because the dates were confusing me.
Evidence Opportunities: A think-aloud during a challenging text: the teacher notes when the student notices a breakdown and what they try next.
Left for June: Monitoring and adjusting consistently in unfamiliar and more complex texts, without stopping-point support.

Skill Descriptor: Reflect and respond personally to a variety of texts across genres, interests, and complexities.
Achievement Indicators:
Preferences: Give generalized explanations of preferences for and personal reactions to particular texts, authors, illustrators, and genres.
Connections: Identify personal experiences and prior knowledge to make personal connections.
Year-End: The student explains their preferences and reactions across texts, authors, illustrators, and genres, and makes personal connections using their experiences and prior knowledge.
Student Statement: I can say what I like to read
Conditions: Self-selected independent reading; literacy identity survey; conversation with the teacher or a partner.
Look Fors:
## Preferences
- Names favourite books, series, or genres, with a simple reason ("It's funny," "There's action").
- Reacts to a text with like or dislike.
## Connections
- Makes connections that are often vague or general ("I have a dog too").
Awareness - Student Quote: I like graphic novels because they're fast to read.
Evidence Opportunities: A literacy identity survey and a first book talk with a partner.
Teacher Note: Int 6.8 covers responses to oral and multimodal texts; this descriptor covers responses to what students read.

Skill Descriptor: Reflect and respond personally to a variety of texts across genres, interests, and complexities.
Achievement Indicators:
Preferences: Give generalized explanations of preferences for and personal reactions to particular texts, authors, illustrators, and genres.
Connections: Identify personal experiences and prior knowledge to make personal connections.
Year-End: The student explains their preferences and reactions across texts, authors, illustrators, and genres, and makes personal connections using their experiences and prior knowledge.
Student Statement: I can explain why a book/text worked for me
Conditions: Independent reading plus at least one teacher-assigned genre they might not choose; reading journal.
Look Fors:
## Preferences
- Explains preferences using features of the text (characters, suspense, art style, how the author writes).
- Gives a reaction to a genre outside typical choice with a reason.
## Connections
- Makes connections to experiences that help them understand a character or event.
- Uses prior knowledge to connect to informational texts.
Awareness - Description: Ties the reaction to the text.
Awareness - Student Quote: I didn't like the poetry unit at first, but the one about the grandma was good because it sounded like how my Nan talks.
Evidence Opportunities: Reading journal entries with a prompt: "What did you think? What part made you think that? What did it remind you of?"
Teacher Note: Int 6.8 covers responses to oral and multimodal texts; this descriptor covers responses to what students read.

Skill Descriptor: Reflect and respond personally to a variety of texts across genres, interests, and complexities.
Achievement Indicators:
Preferences: Give generalized explanations of preferences for and personal reactions to particular texts, authors, illustrators, and genres.
Connections: Identify personal experiences and prior knowledge to make personal connections.
Year-End: The student explains their preferences and reactions across texts, authors, illustrators, and genres, and makes personal connections using their experiences and prior knowledge.
Student Statement: I can notice patterns in what I like and why
Conditions: A range of genres and complexities read across the year; reading tracking/ladder available for reflection.
Look Fors:
## Preferences
- Gives generalized explanations of preferences across authors, illustrators, or genres ("I like authors who...").
- Recommends a text to a specific peer with a reason.
## Connections
- Makes connections that deepen understanding, though some still stay at surface level.
Awareness - Student Quote: I always like books where the main character has to figure it out alone.
Evidence Opportunities: A book recommendation talk or card for a classmate, plus a reading tracker/ladder reflection: "What patterns do you notice in what you liked this year?"
Left for June: Consistently explaining preferences and making meaningful connections across genres and complexities, not only favourites.
Teacher Note: Int 6.8 covers responses to oral and multimodal texts; this descriptor covers responses to what students read.

Skill Descriptor: Independently select, read, and examine critically a variety of texts representing all voices.
Achievement Indicators:
Interpretations: Explain the interpretation of a text through: (1) literary elements (plot, setting, characters, conflict). (2) differentiating claims supported by fact from those that are not.
Perspectives: Evaluate how perspective affects a variety of literary and informational texts by identifying whose voices are present and whose are missing.
Year-End: The student independently selects and reads a variety of texts, explains an interpretation using literary elements, separates supported claims from unsupported ones, and evaluates how perspective shapes a text by noticing whose voices are present and missing.
Student Statement: I can name the parts of a story and check a claim
Conditions: Teacher-curated choices representing a range of voices; short stories and short informational texts; guided discussion.
Look Fors:
## Interpretations
- Identifies plot, setting, main characters, and the main conflict.
- Sorts simple statements into fact and opinion, with examples modelled.
## Perspectives
- Identifies who is telling the story or who wrote the text.
Awareness - Student Quote: The conflict is that he wants to play hockey but his dad says no.
Evidence Opportunities: A story map for a short story, plus a fact/opinion sort using sentences from an article.

Skill Descriptor: Independently select, read, and examine critically a variety of texts representing all voices.
Achievement Indicators:
Interpretations: Explain the interpretation of a text through: (1) literary elements (plot, setting, characters, conflict). (2) differentiating claims supported by fact from those that are not.
Perspectives: Evaluate how perspective affects a variety of literary and informational texts by identifying whose voices are present and whose are missing.
Year-End: The student independently selects and reads a variety of texts, explains an interpretation using literary elements, separates supported claims from unsupported ones, and evaluates how perspective shapes a text by noticing whose voices are present and missing.
Student Statement: I can use the story's parts to explain what it means
Conditions: Choice from a curated set with diverse voices; longer texts, including novels in progress; small-group discussion.
Look Fors:
## Interpretations
- Explains an interpretation using one or two literary elements ("The setting being so cold shows how alone she feels").
- Identifies whether a claim in an informational text is backed by facts, and points to them.
## Perspectives
- Identifies whose voices are present in a text.
- Begins to ask whose voice is missing, when prompted.
Awareness - Student Quote: It's all from the settlers' side. We don't hear what the Wolastoqiyik thought.
Evidence Opportunities: A literature-circle discussion with a "perspective detective" role: "Whose story is this? Who else was there?"

Skill Descriptor: Independently select, read, and examine critically a variety of texts representing all voices.
Achievement Indicators:
