Perspectives: Evaluate how perspective affects a variety of literary and informational texts by identifying whose voices are present and whose are missing.
Year-End: The student independently selects and reads a variety of texts, explains an interpretation using literary elements, separates supported claims from unsupported ones, and evaluates how perspective shapes a text by noticing whose voices are present and missing.
Student Statement: I can think about whose story is being told
Conditions: Students select texts from a wide, diverse library with some guidance; literary and informational texts.
Look Fors:
## Interpretations
- Explains an interpretation using several literary elements, with text evidence.
- Differentiates supported from unsupported claims, though may miss subtle ones.
## Perspectives
- Identifies missing voices with less prompting and begins to explain how the text would change if they were included.
Awareness - Student Quote: If the article talked to the kids who live there, it might not sound like such a good idea.
Evidence Opportunities: A short written or oral response to a self-selected text: an interpretation with evidence, plus "Whose voice is missing? How would the text change with it?"
Left for June: Independent selection across a full range of voices, and evaluating, not just noticing, how perspective shapes a text.

Skill Descriptor: Explore the characteristics, language, form, features, and genres of a range of texts.
Achievement Indicators:
Text Features (Literary Knowledge): Recognize common text structures, such as sequential, description, problem/solution, cause/effect, compare/contrast, and narrative and use them to build meaning.
Text Impact (Author's Craft): Identify choices made by a writer to achieve a stated or implied purpose.
Year-End: The student recognizes common text structures across a range of texts and uses them to build meaning, and identifies a writer's choices that serve a stated or implied purpose.
Student Statement: I can tell how a text is organized
Conditions: Clear examples of narrative, sequential, and description structures; signal-word charts.
Look Fors:
## Text Features
- Recognizes narrative, sequential, and description structures using signal words (first, then, finally; for example).
- Identifies basic text features (headings, captions, bold words) and what they're for.
## Text Impact
- Identifies an obvious writer choice when it is pointed out (a cliffhanger ending, a bold heading).
Awareness - Student Quote: It's in a sequential order, because it says first, next, and last.
Evidence Opportunities: A structure sort: short passages matched to structure names, with the signal words highlighted.

Skill Descriptor: Explore the characteristics, language, form, features, and genres of a range of texts.
Achievement Indicators:
Text Features (Literary Knowledge): Recognize common text structures, such as sequential, description, problem/solution, cause/effect, compare/contrast, and narrative and use them to build meaning.
Text Impact (Author's Craft): Identify choices made by a writer to achieve a stated or implied purpose.
Year-End: The student recognizes common text structures across a range of texts and uses them to build meaning, and identifies a writer's choices that serve a stated or implied purpose.
Student Statement: I can use the structure to help me understand
Conditions: Adds problem/solution, cause/effect, and compare/contrast; mentor texts across genres.
Look Fors:
## Text Features
- Recognizes all six common structures in clear examples.
- Chooses a matching organizer to take notes (a T-chart for compare/contrast).
## Text Impact
- Identifies a writer's choice (word choice, a question to open, a repeated line) and the stated purpose it serves.
Awareness - Student Quote: It's cause and effect, so I looked for what made the flooding happen.
Evidence Opportunities: Read an informational article; identify the structure, complete a matching organizer, and summarize using it.

Skill Descriptor: Explore the characteristics, language, form, features, and genres of a range of texts.
Achievement Indicators:
Text Features (Literary Knowledge): Recognize common text structures, such as sequential, description, problem/solution, cause/effect, compare/contrast, and narrative and use them to build meaning.
Text Impact (Author's Craft): Identify choices made by a writer to achieve a stated or implied purpose.
Year-End: The student recognizes common text structures across a range of texts and uses them to build meaning, and identifies a writer's choices that serve a stated or implied purpose.
Student Statement: I can see why a writer made a choice
Conditions: Varied texts, some mixing structures; purposes not always stated.
Look Fors:
## Text Features
- Identifies the main structure in mixed-structure texts and uses it to build meaning, with some support.
## Text Impact
- Identifies writer choices that serve an implied purpose, with prompting ("Why do you think the author did that?").
- Connects craft noticed in reading to their own writing (links to Rep 6.19).
Awareness - Student Quote: She described the house as falling apart so we'd feel sorry for the family before we even met them.
Evidence Opportunities: A mentor-text study: "Find one choice the author made. What was the author trying to do? Did it work?"
Left for June: Independently using structures in mixed texts, and identifying choices for implied purposes without prompting.

Skill Descriptor: Develop strategies to enhance clarity in multi-modal works.
Achievement Indicators:
Identity: Identify strengths as a writer and collaboratively set goals for improvement with teacher input.
Intention: Begin to demonstrate initiative by bringing ideas from their experiences.
Development: Use writing and design processes to plan, develop, and create engaging and meaningful texts with guidance.
Response: Identify craft moves in the writing of others and self through guided reflection and conferences.
Year-End: The student names strengths and sets goals with the teacher, brings ideas from their own experience, uses a writing and design process with guidance to create engaging texts, and identifies craft moves in their own and others' work through reflection and conferences.
Student Statement: I can talk about myself as a writer
Conditions: Launch of writing workshop; teacher-led conferences; process steps modelled one at a time.
Look Fors:
## Identity
- Names a general strength or struggle ("I'm good at ideas," "I hate spelling"); agrees to a goal the teacher suggests.
## Intention
- Chooses topics from experience when given a list or a heart map.
## Development
- Follows the steps of a process (plan, draft, revise) when guided; revision is mostly fixing errors.
## Response
- Identifies a craft move in a mentor text when it is named ("Find a strong verb").
Awareness - Student Quote: I'm good at stories, but my endings are bad.
Evidence Opportunities: A literacy identity survey, a heart map or idea list, and a first conference note recording one strength and one goal.

Skill Descriptor: Develop strategies to enhance clarity in multi-modal works.
Achievement Indicators:
Identity: Identify strengths as a writer and collaboratively set goals for improvement with teacher input.
Intention: Begin to demonstrate initiative by bringing ideas from their experiences.
Development: Use writing and design processes to plan, develop, and create engaging and meaningful texts with guidance.
Response: Identify craft moves in the writing of others and self through guided reflection and conferences.
Year-End: The student names strengths and sets goals with the teacher, brings ideas from their own experience, uses a writing and design process with guidance to create engaging texts, and identifies craft moves in their own and others' work through reflection and conferences.
Student Statement: I can set a goal and work on it
Conditions: Regular conferences; mentor texts; planning and revision tools available; some multimodal work.
Look Fors:
## Identity
- Names a specific strength with an example; co-sets a goal with the teacher.
## Intention
- Brings their own ideas from experience without a list, most of the time.
## Development
- Plans with an organizer or storyboard and revises for one aspect of clarity (adding detail, reordering), with guidance.
## Response
- Identifies a craft move in a mentor text and tries it in their own work.
Awareness - Description: Names a craft move they tried.
Awareness - Student Quote: I tried starting with dialogue like the book we read.
Evidence Opportunities: A draft with a revision note ("What I changed and why"), and a conference record showing progress on the goal.

Skill Descriptor: Develop strategies to enhance clarity in multi-modal works.
Achievement Indicators:
Identity: Identify strengths as a writer and collaboratively set goals for improvement with teacher input.
Intention: Begin to demonstrate initiative by bringing ideas from their experiences.
Development: Use writing and design processes to plan, develop, and create engaging and meaningful texts with guidance.
Response: Identify craft moves in the writing of others and self through guided reflection and conferences.
Year-End: The student names strengths and sets goals with the teacher, brings ideas from their own experience, uses a writing and design process with guidance to create engaging texts, and identifies craft moves in their own and others' work through reflection and conferences.
Student Statement: I can use the process to make my work clearer
Conditions: Longer and multimodal projects; conferences shared between teacher and peers; process tools chosen by the student.
Look Fors:
## Identity
- Reflects on progress toward a goal and suggests the next one in the conference.
## Intention
- Shows initiative in shaping ideas from experience into a piece, with occasional support.
## Development
- Uses planning and revision to improve clarity, including in design choices (layout, images, headings); still relies on guidance at some stages.
## Response
- Identifies craft moves in their own and peers' work during guided reflection, using shared vocabulary.
Awareness - Student Quote: I moved the picture next to the step it shows so people don't get confused.
Evidence Opportunities: A portfolio piece with planning, draft, and final, plus a reflection: "What strategy made this clearer? What craft move are you proud of?"
Left for June: Applying process strategies across new forms and multimodal works, and naming craft moves with less guidance.

Skill Descriptor: Create a variety of texts with purpose and understand the influence of the writer/creator.
Achievement Indicators:
Topic / Idea: Define a simple and clear topic or idea.
Development: Develop the topic/idea with details and/or examples.
Reasoning: Present predictable and straightforward reasoning.
Year-End: The student independently creates a variety of texts with a clear idea, supporting details, and straightforward reasoning, and explains how a writer's choices influence the reader.
Student Statement: I can say what my writing is about
Conditions: One familiar form, short pieces, sentence frames available.
Look Fors:
## Topic / Idea
- States a clear topic or main idea in a sentence or two.
- Stays on topic for most of the piece, with occasional drift.
## Development
- Adds some relevant details, often list-like ("Dogs are loyal. Also, dogs can be fun.").
- Relies on general details more than specific ones.
## Reasoning
- Gives a simple "because" for an opinion or explanation.
- Connects ideas mostly with and, because, so.
Awareness - Description: Names the purpose (to tell, explain, or convince) and audience when asked.
Awareness - Student Quote: I wanted to convince my teacher that she should move the test to tomorrow.
Evidence Opportunities: A short opinion paragraph on a familiar topic with a frame for the claim, or a snapshot narrative, and an exit question: "What were you trying to do in this piece?"

Skill Descriptor: Create a variety of texts with purpose and understand the influence of the writer/creator.
Achievement Indicators:
Topic / Idea: Define a simple and clear topic or idea.
Development: Develop the topic/idea with details and/or examples.
Reasoning: Present predictable and straightforward reasoning.
Year-End: The student independently creates a variety of texts with a clear idea, supporting details, and straightforward reasoning, and explains how a writer's choices influence the reader.
Student Statement: I can build my idea so it makes sense to someone else
Conditions: Two or more forms, multi-paragraph pieces, less scaffolding.
Look Fors:
## Topic / Idea
- Narrows a broad topic to a focused one ("pets" becomes "why older dogs make good first pets").
- Keeps the focus through a multi-paragraph piece.
## Development
- Chooses details that support the topic, not just relate to it.
- Uses some specific details: a named example, a small anecdote, a fact.
- Begins grouping related details into paragraphs.
## Reasoning
- Links reasons to the claim and explains how a detail supports it ("This shows that...").
- Uses a predictable order and transitions beyond and/so.
Awareness - Description: Notices how a mentor text's choices affect them as a reader.
Awareness - Student Quote: The author started with a story, so I wanted to keep reading.
Evidence Opportunities: The same topic written in two forms (e.g. informational and persuasive), with a short reflection on what changed.

Skill Descriptor: Create a variety of texts with purpose and understand the influence of the writer/creator.
Achievement Indicators:
Topic / Idea: Define a simple and clear topic or idea.
Development: Develop the topic/idea with details and/or examples.
Reasoning: Present predictable and straightforward reasoning.
Year-End: The student independently creates a variety of texts with a clear idea, supporting details, and straightforward reasoning, and explains how a writer's choices influence the reader.
Student Statement: I can write with a clear idea, support it, and start to explain my choices
Conditions: Familiar forms independently; newer forms with some support.
Look Fors:
## Topic / Idea
- Defines a clear, focused idea mostly independently in familiar forms; may need help narrowing in a new form.
## Development
- Uses relevant, mostly specific details; elaboration is strong in places and thin in others.
## Reasoning
- Reasoning is predictable and straightforward in familiar forms, and may weaken in less practised ones.
Awareness - Description: Explains why a form or one key choice fits the purpose, with a prompt, and identifies what a creator wants an audience to think or feel in a familiar text type.
Awareness - Student Quote: I started with a question so the reader would want to know the answer.
Evidence Opportunities: A piece in a form the student chooses for a given purpose, plus a short writer's note on one choice and its intended effect. Optionally, a response to an ad: "What does the creator want you to believe?"
Left for June: Consistency across a variety of texts, explaining choices independently, and explaining a writer's influence in less familiar forms.

Skill Descriptor: Select an appropriate form that reflects audience, purpose, and topic.
Achievement Indicators:
Structure: Choose basic organizational structures.
Sequence: Arrange ideas in an understandable or helpful order.
Transition: Group ideas using formulaic, predictable transitions.
Leads/Conclusions: Provide leads and conclusions, but they are obvious and formulaic.
Year-End: The student chooses a basic form and structure that suits the audience, purpose, and topic, orders ideas helpfully, groups them with predictable transitions, and includes a lead and conclusion, even if formulaic.
Student Statement: I can put my writing in an order that makes sense
Conditions: One familiar form; structure provided (e.g., a paragraph frame or story arc).
Look Fors:
## Structure
- Uses the structure provided.
## Sequence
- Ideas are in a mostly logical order, with some jumps.
## Transition
- Uses a few basic transitions (first, then, also) or none.
## Leads/Conclusions
- A lead or conclusion may be missing, or is a single generic line ("This is about..." / "The end").
Awareness - Student Quote: I wrote it in the order it happened.
Evidence Opportunities: A short piece in a familiar form; check against a four-part structure checklist (structure, sequence, transitions, lead/conclusion).
Teacher Note: The indicators describe a June standard that is intentionally formulaic ("obvious," "predictable"). On-track April work should look formulaic too; the growth is in using these elements reliably, not in making them sophisticated.

Skill Descriptor: Select an appropriate form that reflects audience, purpose, and topic.
Achievement Indicators:
Structure: Choose basic organizational structures.
Sequence: Arrange ideas in an understandable or helpful order.
Transition: Group ideas using formulaic, predictable transitions.
Leads/Conclusions: Provide leads and conclusions, but they are obvious and formulaic.
Year-End: The student chooses a basic form and structure that suits the audience, purpose, and topic, orders ideas helpfully, groups them with predictable transitions, and includes a lead and conclusion, even if formulaic.
Student Statement: I can choose how to organize my writing
Conditions: Two or three forms taught (narrative, procedural, opinion); a choice between two structures.
Look Fors:
## Structure
- Chooses between two given structures to fit the purpose, with support.
## Sequence
- Orders ideas in a helpful way across paragraphs (chronological, most to least important).
## Transition
- Uses transitions to group ideas, mostly from a list.
## Leads/Conclusions
- Includes both, usually formulaic (a question, "In conclusion...").
Awareness - Student Quote: I used steps because I'm teaching how to do it.
Evidence Opportunities: Same topic, two forms (e.g., a how-to and a story); a reflection on why each structure fits.
Teacher Note: The indicators describe a June standard that is intentionally formulaic ("obvious," "predictable"). On-track April work should look formulaic too; the growth is in using these elements reliably, not in making them sophisticated.

Skill Descriptor: Select an appropriate form that reflects audience, purpose, and topic.
Achievement Indicators:
Structure: Choose basic organizational structures.
Sequence: Arrange ideas in an understandable or helpful order.
Transition: Group ideas using formulaic, predictable transitions.
Leads/Conclusions: Provide leads and conclusions, but they are obvious and formulaic.
Year-End: The student chooses a basic form and structure that suits the audience, purpose, and topic, orders ideas helpfully, groups them with predictable transitions, and includes a lead and conclusion, even if formulaic.
Student Statement: I can pick a form that fits my purpose and audience
Conditions: Several forms available, including multimodal; the student chooses the form for a given purpose and audience
Look Fors:
## Structure
- Chooses a basic form and structure that suits audience, purpose, and topic, with some prompting.
## Sequence
- Arranges ideas in a helpful order through most of the piece.
## Transition
- Uses predictable transitions to group ideas, mostly independently.
## Leads/Conclusions
- Includes a lead and conclusion in most pieces; both are obvious and formulaic.
Awareness - Student Quote: I made it a poster because it's for little kids, and they need pictures.
Evidence Opportunities: A purpose-and-audience prompt with free choice of form; a planning sheet showing the chosen form and structure.
Left for June: Choosing the form independently, and consistent sequence, transitions, leads, and conclusions across the variety of forms taught.
Teacher Note: The indicators describe a June standard that is intentionally formulaic ("obvious," "predictable"). On-track April work should look formulaic too; the growth is in using these elements reliably, not in making them sophisticated.

Skill Descriptor: Include interesting and/or domain-specific words and phrases to convey and enhance meaning.
Achievement Indicators:
Specific & Accurate Words: Show mastery of functional and familiar words.
Striking Words & Phrases: Use sensory details to create imagery.
Deepening Meaning: Choose words that are appropriate for the audience and text type, and the purpose can be identified.
Year-End: The student uses functional and familiar words accurately, adds sensory details that create imagery, and chooses words suited to the audience and text type so the purpose is clear.
Student Statement: I can use words that say what I mean
Conditions: Familiar topics; short pieces; word banks and mentor sentences available.
Look Fors:
## Specific & Accurate Words
- Uses familiar words correctly, with some general or repeated words (good, nice, stuff, went).
## Striking Words & Phrases
- Adds a sensory detail when prompted ("What did it sound like?"), usually sight.
## Deepening Meaning
- Word choice is mostly the same across forms.
Awareness - Description: Notices a better word when shown.
Awareness - Student Quote: 'Sprinted' is better than 'ran fast.'
Evidence Opportunities: A short descriptive paragraph; students circle three words they chose on purpose.

Skill Descriptor: Include interesting and/or domain-specific words and phrases to convey and enhance meaning.
Achievement Indicators:
Specific & Accurate Words: Show mastery of functional and familiar words.
Striking Words & Phrases: Use sensory details to create imagery.
Deepening Meaning: Choose words that are appropriate for the audience and text type, and the purpose can be identified.
Year-End: The student uses functional and familiar words accurately, adds sensory details that create imagery, and chooses words suited to the audience and text type so the purpose is clear.
Student Statement: I can choose words that help the reader picture it
Conditions: Narrative, descriptive, and informational pieces; mentor texts; domain vocabulary from content units.
Look Fors:
## Specific & Accurate Words
- Replaces some general words with more specific ones during revision.
- Uses topic vocabulary from a unit accurately in informational writing.
## Striking Words & Phrases
- Uses sensory details from more than one sense to build an image in a key moment.
## Deepening Meaning
- Begins to choose different word styles for different text types (story vs. report).
Awareness - Student Quote: I said 'the floor creaked' so you'd hear it and know someone was coming.
Evidence Opportunities: A revision task: highlight five general words in a draft and revise three; note the effect.

Skill Descriptor: Include interesting and/or domain-specific words and phrases to convey and enhance meaning.
Achievement Indicators:
Specific & Accurate Words: Show mastery of functional and familiar words.
Striking Words & Phrases: Use sensory details to create imagery.
Deepening Meaning: Choose words that are appropriate for the audience and text type, and the purpose can be identified.
Year-End: The student uses functional and familiar words accurately, adds sensory details that create imagery, and chooses words suited to the audience and text type so the purpose is clear.
Student Statement: I can choose words that fit my reader and my purpose
Conditions: A variety of forms for real audiences; less scaffolding; word banks optional.
Look Fors:
## Specific & Accurate Words
- Uses functional and familiar words accurately throughout, with few general fillers.
## Striking Words & Phrases
- Uses sensory details to create imagery in narrative and descriptive pieces, sometimes overdoing it.
## Deepening Meaning
- Chooses words that suit the audience and text type in planned pieces; the purpose is identifiable to a reader.
Awareness - Student Quote: I used 'habitat' in the report because it's science, but in the letter to my cousin I just said 'where they live.'
Evidence Opportunities: Two short pieces on one topic for two audiences or text types, with a note on the words they changed and why.
Left for June: Consistently appropriate word choice across all forms, and imagery that serves the piece without being overdone.

Skill Descriptor: Provide evidence of author's style, personality, and experience.
Achievement Indicators:
Audience Engagement: Connect the audience to the topic/idea and purpose.
Tone: Use an appropriate tone for the audience and purpose.
Commitment: Commit to the topic and purpose with some vague generalities.
Style: Experiment with point of view and perspective.
Year-End: The student's writing connects the reader to the topic and purpose, uses an appropriate tone, shows commitment to the topic (with some vague generalities), and experiments with point of view and perspective.
Student Statement: I can write about something I care about
Conditions: Self-chosen topics from experience; personal narrative or opinion; first person.
Look Fors:
## Audience Engagement
- Writing is mostly for themselves or the teacher; occasional direct address to the reader.
## Tone
- Tone is natural and conversational; doesn't yet shift for audience or purpose.
## Commitment
- Interest in the topic shows in places, mixed with many general statements ("It was really fun").
## Style
- Writes from their own first-person point of view.
Awareness - Description: Names why they chose the topic.
Awareness - Student Quote: I wrote about my camp because it's my favourite place.
Evidence Opportunities: A personal narrative or "small moment" piece; a partner reads it and says, "I can tell you care about this because..."
Teacher Note: Like 6.21, the Commitment indicator accepts "some vague generalities" in June. April writing will have more of them; that is on track.

Skill Descriptor: Provide evidence of author's style, personality, and experience.
Achievement Indicators:
Audience Engagement: Connect the audience to the topic/idea and purpose.
Tone: Use an appropriate tone for the audience and purpose.
Commitment: Commit to the topic and purpose with some vague generalities.
Style: Experiment with point of view and perspective.
Year-End: The student's writing connects the reader to the topic and purpose, uses an appropriate tone, shows commitment to the topic (with some vague generalities), and experiments with point of view and perspective.
Student Statement: I can sound like me and keep my reader interested
Conditions: Mix of personal and assigned topics; mentor texts with strong voice.
Look Fors:
## Audience Engagement
- Uses a hook or direct address to bring the reader in.
## Tone
- Recognizes when a tone is too casual or too stiff for a purpose and adjusts with feedback.
## Commitment
- Stays with the topic and includes some specific personal details.
## Style
- Tries a different point of view in a short task (e.g., retelling from another character's view).
Awareness - Student Quote: You can tell it's me because I made a joke like I would.
Evidence Opportunities: A point-of-view rewrite: retell a familiar event from a different perspective, with a reflection on what changed.
Teacher Note: Like 6.21, the Commitment indicator accepts "some vague generalities" in June. April writing will have more of them; that is on track.

Skill Descriptor: Provide evidence of author's style, personality, and experience.
Achievement Indicators:
Audience Engagement: Connect the audience to the topic/idea and purpose.
Tone: Use an appropriate tone for the audience and purpose.
Commitment: Commit to the topic and purpose with some vague generalities.
Style: Experiment with point of view and perspective.
Year-End: The student's writing connects the reader to the topic and purpose, uses an appropriate tone, shows commitment to the topic (with some vague generalities), and experiments with point of view and perspective.
Student Statement: I can choose a tone and point of view on purpose
Conditions: Varied forms and audiences; choice of point of view in some tasks.
Look Fors:
## Audience Engagement
- Connects the reader to the topic and purpose in most pieces, especially at the start.
## Tone
- Chooses a tone that fits the audience and purpose in planned pieces; it may drift partway through.
## Commitment
- Shows commitment to the topic, with some vague generalities.
## Style
- Experiments with point of view or perspective in a piece of their choosing.
Awareness - Description: Explains a tone or POV choice.
Awareness - Student Quote: I wrote it as the dog so it would be funny and people would want to adopt one.
Evidence Opportunities: A piece with an author's note: "Who is your reader? What tone did you choose? Why that point of view?"
Left for June: Holding tone steady through a whole piece, and experimenting with point of view across forms, not just in a chosen task.
Teacher Note: Like 6.21, the Commitment indicator accepts "some vague generalities" in June. April writing will have more of them; that is on track.

Skill Descriptor: Include well-crafted sentences to support meaning and readability.
Achievement Indicators:
Crafted Structure: Construct proper, simple, and compound sentences while experimenting with complex sentence structure.
Variety: Use routine and/or a generic variety of sentence lengths and beginnings.
Rhythm: Create a rhythm that is pleasant/professional but feels mechanical at times.
Year-End: The student writes correct simple and compound sentences, experiments with complex ones, varies sentence lengths and beginnings in routine ways, and produces writing that reads pleasantly, if mechanically at times.
Student Statement: I can write complete sentences
Conditions: Short pieces; sentence-combining practice; mentor sentences.
Look Fors:
## Crafted Structure
- Writes mostly complete sentences; some run-ons or fragments.
- Joins ideas with and or and then, sometimes repeatedly.
## Variety
- Many sentences start the same way (I, Then, The) and are similar in length.
## Rhythm
- Writing reads as choppy or run-together in places.
Awareness - Description: Hears a problem when reading aloud.
Awareness - Student Quote: That sentence is too long, I ran out of breath.
Evidence Opportunities: A writing sample analyzed for sentence types and first words; a read-aloud to a partner.

Skill Descriptor: Include well-crafted sentences to support meaning and readability.
Achievement Indicators:
Crafted Structure: Construct proper, simple, and compound sentences while experimenting with complex sentence structure.
Variety: Use routine and/or a generic variety of sentence lengths and beginnings.
Rhythm: Create a rhythm that is pleasant/professional but feels mechanical at times.
Year-End: The student writes correct simple and compound sentences, experiments with complex ones, varies sentence lengths and beginnings in routine ways, and produces writing that reads pleasantly, if mechanically at times.
Student Statement: I can combine and change up my sentences
Conditions: Sentence-combining and sentence-starter mini-lessons; revision checklists.
Look Fors:
## Crafted Structure
- Writes correct compound sentences using FANBOYS conjunctions (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so).
- Tries a complex sentence with a familiar connector (because, when, if, after).
## Variety
- Varies sentence beginnings during revision using a list of starters.
- Mixes some short and long sentences.
## Rhythm
- Fewer choppy or run-together stretches; reads aloud to check flow when prompted.
Awareness - Student Quote: I put two short ones together with 'but' because they were about the same thing.
Evidence Opportunities: A before-and-after revision of a paragraph, highlighting combined sentences and new beginnings.

Skill Descriptor: Include well-crafted sentences to support meaning and readability.
Achievement Indicators:
Crafted Structure: Construct proper, simple, and compound sentences while experimenting with complex sentence structure.
Variety: Use routine and/or a generic variety of sentence lengths and beginnings.
Rhythm: Create a rhythm that is pleasant/professional but feels mechanical at times.
Year-End: The student writes correct simple and compound sentences, experiments with complex ones, varies sentence lengths and beginnings in routine ways, and produces writing that reads pleasantly, if mechanically at times.
Student Statement: I can make my sentences sound good together
Conditions: Longer pieces in varied forms; read-aloud and peer feedback built into revision.
Look Fors:
## Crafted Structure
- Writes correct simple and compound sentences consistently; complex sentences are attempted, sometimes with errors.
## Variety
- Uses a routine variety of lengths and beginnings, sometimes in a predictable pattern.
## Rhythm
